Executive Summary 
The World Energy Investment 2024 report provides an update on the investment picture in the energy sector in 2023 and an initial reading of the emerging investment picture for 2024. The report is a global benchmark for tracking capital flows in the energy sector and examines how investors are assessing risks and opportunities across all areas of fuel and electricity supply, critical minerals, energy efficiency, research and development, and energy finance.

Key findings from the report include:

* Global energy investment declined by 13% in 2023, to USD 1.8 trillion, as a result of reduced spending on fossil fuels and lower investment in critical minerals, which more than offset increases in spending on clean energy and energy efficiency.
* Clean energy investments, including renewables, energy efficiency, and electric vehicles, rose by 14% in 2023, to USD 900 billion, accounting for 50% of total investment in the energy sector. Fossil fuel investments, including upstream oil and gas, LNG, and coal, fell by 26% to USD 689 billion, a record low.
* The share of clean energy investments in total energy investment reached a record high of 50% in 2023, up from 45% in 2022. The share of fossil fuel investments in total energy investment fell to a record low of 38%, down from 45% in 2022.
* Renewable energy investments rose by 21% in 2023, to USD 450 billion, driven by strong growth in solar PV, offshore wind, and batteries. The share of renewable energy investments in total energy investment reached 25%, up from 21% in 2022.
* Energy efficiency investments rose by 8% in 2023, to USD 450 billion, driven by strong growth in building retrofits and appliances. The share of energy efficiency investments in total energy investment reached 25%, up from 23% in 2022.
* The decline in fossil fuel investments in 2023 was driven by reduced spending on upstream oil and gas, LNG, and coal. Upstream oil and gas investments fell by 26%, to USD 273 billion, the lowest level since 2016. LNG investments fell by 29%, to USD 137 billion, the lowest level since 2017. Coal investments fell by 17%, to USD 79 billion, the lowest level since 2010.
* Investment in critical minerals, including rare earth elements, cobalt, and lithium, fell by 16% in 2023, to USD 191 billion, due to lower demand for electric vehicles and reduced investment in renewable energy projects.
* The World Energy Investment 2024 report also provides an expanded analysis on the sources of investment and sources of finance in the energy sector, including new insights on the role of development finance institutions in energy investments across emerging and developing economies. It also looks at how investment trends in clean energy compare with those in fossil fuels, as well as the geographic distribution of these investments.
* The report also includes a new regional section covering 10 major economies and regions, including the United States, China, Europe, India, Japan, the Middle East, Latin America, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific. It provides a comprehensive assessment of the investment picture in each region and identifies key trends and challenges.
* The report also assesses additional efforts needed to meet the COP28 goals to transition away from fossil fuels, triple renewable capacity, and double the rate of improvements in energy efficiency by 2030.

The World Energy Investment 2024 report highlights several key aspects of the current investment landscape, including persistent cost and interest rate pressures, the new industrial strategies being adopted by major economies to boost clean energy manufacturing, and the policies that support incentives for clean energy spending, notably from the increasingly important viewpoints of energy security and affordability.

The report also provides an initial reading of the emerging investment picture for 2024. Based on current trends, it is expected that investment in clean energy will continue to grow, driven by strong demand for renewable energy and energy efficiency projects. However, the report also notes that the outlook for fossil fuel investments remains uncertain, due to ongoing price volatility and policy uncertainty.

Overall, the World Energy Investment 2024 report provides a comprehensive and data-driven assessment of the investment picture in the energy sector and identifies key trends and challenges. It is an essential resource for policymakers, investors, and stakeholders who are interested in understanding the latest developments in the energy sector and shaping the path towards a more sustainable and secure energy future.

be further broken down into mass transport losses in the
electrode, the mass transport losses in the membrane and
the mass transport losses in the gas flow channels. The
presentation will include the underlying fundamental
physics and chemistry, experimental results in support of
these phenomena, the present state-of-the-art and the poten-
tial for further improvements.
The discussion will address the efﬁciencies of the various
loss mechanisms, i.e., the degree of reversibility of the
loss-related phenomena, which represents the potential
for process simpliﬁcation of the fuel cell system design.
Additional efﬁciency losses (and their potential for process

The article will conclude with an overview of the state-

simpliﬁcation of the fuel cell system, i.e., a 100 kW fuel

Clearly, this goal for MEA performance is far from being

The overall performance of a fuel cell is described by the

The performance equation includes seven loss mechanisms
and their corresponding voltage drops:
(i)
Activation losses (ΔVact) due to the sluggish kinetics
of the electrochemical reactions at the electrode sur-

(ii)
Ohmic losses (ΔVohm) due to the ohmic resistance of the

(iii)
Mass transport losses (ΔVmass) due to the slow trans-

(iv)
Membrane transport losses (ΔVmem) due to the slow
transport of the reactants and the water from the elec-
trode surfaces through the membrane and the membrane
electrode interface (MEI) to the gas channels.
(v)
Concentration losses (ΔVconc) due to the depletion of
the reactants at the electrode surfaces and the resulting
change in the reaction rate.
(vi)
Diffusion losses (ΔVdiff) due to the depletion of the
reactants within the electrode structure and the resulting
change in the reaction rate.
(vii)
Stray current losses (ΔVstray) due to the formation of
electrolyte ions within the gas channels.
In the derivation of the performance equation, the losses
due to the heat removal have been neglected, since they
are usually small compared to the other losses. However,
for fuel cells at high current densities the heat removal
becomes more important and needs to be considered.[9, 10]
The reversibility of the loss mechanisms can be inferred
from the performance equation. In the absence of losses,
the cell voltage Vcell is equal to the MEA voltage, indicating
a reversible loss mechanism. On the other hand, if a loss
mechanism is irreversible, the corresponding voltage drop
VVi is constant and independent of the other losses.
The reversibility of the loss mechanisms is of particular
interest, since it allows for the simpliﬁcation of the fuel
cell system design. For example, the reversibility of the
mass transport losses (ΔVmass) allows for the simpliﬁcation
of the humidification of the reactant gas streams, since the
mass transport losses can be recovered by adjusting the
reactant flow rates.
The reversibility of the loss mechanisms is also a key
factor for the development of MEA with increased perfor-
mance. Whereas irreversible losses cannot be recovered,
reversible losses represent an opportunity for the fuel cell
manufacturer to increase the MEA performance without
increasing the cost of the fuel cell system.
